Project explainer · November 2026

Bharat Health Intelligence

One health record per person, read by AI and checked by doctors, with early warnings when a patient starts to get worse. The plan is to prove it first in Telangana, in 100 days.

ప్రతి కుటుంబానికి ఒక ఆరోగ్య రికార్డు

Built from two concept decks, for the meeting with the Chief Minister's Office in early December 2026. Nothing has been built yet. All screens and numbers in the decks are mock-ups.

100days for the Telangana proof of concept
5building blocks: records, AI, wearables, emergency, dashboards
3first languages: English, Hindi, Telugu
2027–32from Hyderabad pilot to national scale

The problem

Your health history is scattered, so care starts late

Most people's records sit on paper slips and in separate hospital systems. A doctor seeing you today rarely sees what happened last year. Warning signs between visits go unnoticed until it is an emergency.

Scattered records

Paper prescriptions, hospital systems that don't talk to each other, and reports in different formats.

No full picture

Neither the patient nor the doctor can see one complete timeline of tests, medicines and visits.

Care that reacts

Rising blood pressure or falling oxygen at home is not seen until the person reaches a hospital.

Missing from the decks: real numbers. Neither deck gives a single figure for the size of this problem in Telangana or India. Before the meeting we need 4 to 6 sourced figures, for example diabetes and hypertension rates in the pilot district, how many records are still on paper, and how long it takes from an abnormal test to a doctor seeing it.

The solution

Collect, clean, connect, read, respond

The system works as a pipeline. It does not build one big central database. Records stay with the hospitals and labs that hold them and are shared only with the patient's consent, using India's national digital health standards (ABDM).

  1. CollectPhotos of paper prescriptions, hospital and lab systems, and readings from smartwatches if the patient agrees.
  2. CleanText is read from images, mapped to standard medical codes, and checked by a person. Every item keeps a note of where it came from.
  3. ConnectRecords are linked into one timeline per person, through ABDM and with consent.
  4. ReadAI writes a short summary, applies clinical rules and flags risk. It points to the source for every statement.
  5. RespondA doctor reviews every alert. The care team is notified and the outcome is recorded.

How an emergency alert moves

Detect→Verify→Notify→Acknowledge→Escalate→Document

No step is automatic diagnosis. A qualified clinician checks the alert before anyone acts on it.

The five building blocks

Health Data GridThe record layer

Turns paper and scattered files into one consented, standard health record per person. This is the foundation everything else needs.

Medical IntelligenceHelp for doctors

Short summaries of a patient's history, prescription reading, medicine interaction checks and risk scores. The doctor accepts, edits or rejects each one.

Wearable IntelligenceReadings from home

Heart rate, oxygen, sleep and activity from watches and bands, compared with the person's own normal range. The deck notes these devices are not medical grade.

Emergency NetworkHospital response

A hospital screen that lists patients at risk in order, shows the evidence, routes to the right team and records who acknowledged what and when.

Population InsightsFor government

District-level counts of disease, screening gaps and demand for staff, beds and medicines. Only grouped data, small numbers hidden, every use audited. No routine access to named patient records.

Who uses it

Same data, a different view for each person

Citizen or patient

Main beneficiary

  • Sees one timeline of visits, tests and medicines.
  • Takes a photo of a prescription; it becomes part of the record after a check.
  • Asks questions by voice in Telugu, Hindi or English.
  • Chooses who can see which records, and for how long. Can withdraw at any time.
  • Optional: links a smartwatch and gets a nudge to see a doctor if readings change.

Doctor

Main clinical user

  • Opens a patient and sees the full history and a short AI summary with sources.
  • Reviews prescription fields the AI has read from a photo.
  • Gets warnings on medicine interactions and suggested next tests.
  • Dictates notes by voice.

Hospital team

Care delivery

  • A command screen lists patients whose condition may be getting worse, most urgent first.
  • Shows the evidence behind each alert and live vitals.
  • Routes to cardiology, ICU or the ER team and logs who acknowledged it.
  • Helps plan beds.

Government

Planning and oversight

  • District and mandal dashboards: disease burden, screening and follow-up gaps.
  • Forecasts of staff, beds and medicines needed.
  • Tracks rollout: facilities connected, records digitised, data quality.
  • Only grouped, privacy-protected data.

Researchers and pharma

Later phase, in the clinical deck only

  • Finds how many eligible patients exist for a study.
  • Matches patients to clinical trials; the trial site makes the final call.
  • Tracks new medicines approved in India and abroad.
  • Genomic reports for cancer care.

Suggest leaving this out of the CM pitch. It widens the scope and raises privacy questions.

ASHA workers and PHC staff Not in decks

The biggest missing user

  • Neither deck mentions frontline public health staff.
  • For a state government, they are who would use this most: follow-up lists after screening, home visit reminders, a simple Telugu voice app.
  • Adding this view would make the pitch about the public system, not only private hospitals.

The roadmap

From 100 days to six years

  1. Day 1–30Set upChoose partners, set up governance, agree use cases and a clinical testing plan.
  2. Day 31–60Build the record layerRecord intake, standard formats, consent, and a simulated wearable feed.
  3. Day 61–80Connect the appsPatient app, doctor portal, hospital alerts and the operations dashboard work together.
  4. Day 81–100Supervised demoRun the full journey with simulated data, test security, measure results.
  1. 2027Hyderabad proof of conceptWith clinical design partners.
  2. 2028District rolloutMixed urban and rural areas.
  3. 2029Statewide demonstrationMore languages, chronic disease care.
  4. 2030More statesModels validated by an independent body.
  5. 2031–32National readinessPartnerships and phased national scale.

What the demo shows: a patient uploads a prescription, AI reads it, a doctor checks it, the timeline updates, a watch reading changes, a risk review starts, the hospital gets an alert, and the team logs what they did.

Simulated patients and device readings only. No live ambulance dispatch.

Mismatch: the clinical deck uses a different plan (0–6, 6–12, 12–24 and 24+ months). The two plans need to become one.

Why it matters for Telangana

Make the state's existing health schemes work as one

The decks name Telangana only for the pilot. The pitch is stronger if it shows how the system helps programmes the state already runs. Every item below needs checking against current facts before the meeting.

Aarogyasri verifyState health insurance

A complete, digitised history could speed up pre-approvals and cut repeat tests for insured families.

T-Diagnostics verifyFree government lab network

Test results go straight into the patient's timeline and the doctor's view. Abnormal results can raise a follow-up task.

Basti Dawakhanas, UPHCs and PHCs verifyNeighbourhood and primary clinics

One doctor sees many patients a day. A photo-to-record prescription and a short summary save time at every visit.

Kanti Velugu and NCD screening verifyMass screening drives

Screening results become follow-up lists for ASHAs, so a camp leads to treatment, not just a count.

108 emergency service verifyAmbulance network

The hospital alert loop can later hand over to 108. The pilot does not dispatch ambulances.

The state's digital health profile work verifyPossible overlap

The current government has announced plans for a digital health profile for citizens. Check its status. Position this project as the AI, voice and alert layer on top of it, not a rival system.

For people

One record per family, a health assistant that speaks Telugu, faster follow-up after a bad test result.

For the government

A live dashboard by district and mandal, a launch the CM can attend in 2027, and a model other states would copy.

What we need from the government

The asks

From the decks

  • Approve clinical partners, POC scope, safety rules and the 100-day plan.
  • One state partner, two hospitals and a clinical advisory group.
  • Approve data access agreements and clinical safety and regulatory reviews.

Also needed, not in the decks

  • A nodal officer in the Health department.
  • One named pilot district, ideally one urban and one rural area.
  • Hosting in a state-approved data centre or cloud.
  • A clear funding source for the POC.
  • A review date at day 100.

Gaps and risks

What to fix before the meeting

No numbers for the problem high

Add sourced Telangana figures. Without them the pitch is a technology idea, not an answer to a state problem.

No cost, funding or team high

Neither deck says what the POC costs, who pays, who builds it, or who owns the result.

Not tied to state programmes or frontline workers high

No mention of Aarogyasri, T-Diagnostics, PHCs or ASHAs. The pitch reads as a private-hospital product.

Two decks, two stories medium
  • Two names: "Bharat Clinical Intelligence" and "Bharat Health Intelligence".
  • Pilot size: 12 districts and 246 facilities in one, 3 districts and 25 facilities in another.
  • Three timelines in different units.
  • "Superintelligence" in a title. Drop it.
Mock-ups look AI-made and use real brands medium

Typos, made-up faces, real hospital names and result-like numbers. Officials may read the numbers as real.

Regulation and safety medium

A patient-facing "high risk in the next 48 hours" alert may count as a medical device under CDSCO rules. Also needed: the DPDP Act consent rules, ABDM certification, and ethics approval for the pilot.

Who benefits from wearables low

Few low-income families own smartwatches. Keep wearables optional and lead with records and follow-up.

For the meeting

Suggested talking points

  1. Start with Telangana, not AI. "We want every family in one district to have a health record they can speak to in Telugu, and every abnormal test to reach a doctor within days."
  2. It strengthens what the government already runs. Aarogyasri, T-Diagnostics, Basti Dawakhanas and ASHAs get one shared record and a follow-up list.
  3. A visible result in 100 days. A working demo, then a district launch the CM can open, with a public dashboard by mandal.
  4. Low risk. Simulated data first, consent for real data, no central database, a doctor checks every alert, the state owns the data.
  5. Telangana leads, India follows. Built in Hyderabad, offered to other states later as the Telangana model.
  6. One clear ask. A nodal officer, one pilot district and data-sharing approval, with a review at day 100.

Avoid saying

superintelligenceaccuracy numbers we haven't measured"diagnoses"hospital partners not yet signed

Open questions

To answer before December

What does the POC cost, and who pays for it?
Which name leads: Bharat Health Intelligence, or a Telangana name for the state version?
What exactly should the CM say yes to: an MoU, a pilot district, a budget, an introduction to the Health department?
